title: A memorandum, step by step
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A clear, short, specific memorandum gets read. A step-by-step guide to structure, demands, follow-up and escalation, with real examples.
body:
Union work runs on paper more than people sometimes admit. A strike, a rally or a delegation draws attention, but what the officer in the ministry actually keeps on file is a **memorandum**: a written statement of the problem and a list of demands. A memorandum that is clear, short and specific can be forwarded, discussed and answered. One that is vague, long or angry is usually acknowledged and forgotten. This guide sets out how to write the first kind, step by step.

## Why a memorandum matters

The Constitution guarantees citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression, the right to assemble peaceably and without arms, and the right to form associations or unions, in Article 19(1)(a), (b) and (c) ([Constitution of India, Article 19](https://constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-19-protection-of-certain-rights-regarding-freedom-of-speech-etc/)). A memorandum is the quiet, everyday use of these rights. It is also the document that proves, months later, that a demand was made, on what date, to whom and in what words. In any later discussion, whether at a tripartite meeting, before a labour authority or in a court, that record can matter.

Workers also have formal channels beyond the ministry's front desk. The Indian Labour Conference, the apex tripartite body in the Ministry of Labour and Employment, brings together Central trade unions, employers' organisations, State Governments and Central ministries. It was first held in 1942, and 46 sessions have taken place, the last in July 2015 ([Drishti IAS explainer](https://www.drishtiias.com/daily-updates/daily-news-analysis/indian-labour-conference); [Business Standard](https://business-standard.com/india-news/house-panel-asks-labour-ministry-to-hold-labour-conference-at-earliest-125041800770_1.html)). A parliamentary standing committee asked the Ministry in 2025 to convene it at the earliest opportunity, and BMS's Central Executive meeting in August 2025 also asked for the Conference to be convened ([BMS press release](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=8936)). A good memorandum often feeds into such forums, even when they do not meet as often as unions would like.

## The structure of a good memorandum

1. **Heading.** The authority it is addressed to (by designation, for example "The Secretary, Ministry of Labour and Employment"), the name of the union and federation sending it, the date, and a one-line subject.
2. **Background.** One paragraph on the problem, who is affected and for how long. Keep it factual.
3. **Facts.** Numbers, dates and documents. Cite the Act, section, rule, notification or order by name and number. If there is a Government order, attach it.
4. **Demands.** Number them. Each one should be a single action that the authority can take.
5. **Request.** Ask for a meeting, and for a reply within a stated time.
6. **Annexures.** List and attach the supporting documents: a wage slip, a circular, a list of affected workers, a newspaper report.
7. **Signatures.** The president and general secretary, with the union's registration number and address.

## Tips from experience

- **One subject per memorandum** where possible. A memorandum that mixes pension, bonus, contract labour and canteen quality gives the officer an excuse to send it to four desks.
- **Use plain language.** Slogans belong on banners. Officers need to know what to do.
- **Name the specific rule or order you want amended** or implemented. For example, instead of asking for "better wages", point to the clause of the order that fixes a rate and say what the rate should be.
- **Fix a date.** "With effect from 1 April" is something an officer can act on. "As soon as possible" is not.
- **Keep copies and proof of delivery.** Get a receiving stamp with the date on your office copy, or send by registered post, or by email with a read receipt as well, and record the diary number.
- **Follow up** with a polite reminder after 15 to 30 days, quoting the date and diary number of the first memorandum.
- **Be accurate.** Check each number before you sign. A single wrong figure can be used to dismiss the whole memorandum.

## A real example of specific demands

Concrete demands are easier to answer. In February 2026, after its triennial conference in Odisha, BMS submitted a memorandum to the Union Government with demands that were stated in numbers. They included raising the minimum pension under EPS-95 from Rs 1,000 to Rs 7,500 per month with dearness relief, raising the EPF coverage ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000 and the ESIC ceiling from Rs 21,000 to Rs 42,000 per month, and raising the Bonus Act ceilings. It also asked for regularisation of scheme and contract workers and for concerns about the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code to be resolved ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/india/rss-affiliate-bms-flags-labour-code-implementation-gaps-seeks-5-day-week-for-banking-sector/2864682)).

Whatever one thinks of any particular demand, the form is instructive: each item names a scheme, a current figure and a requested figure. On 17 September 2026 the Labour Ministry notified a revised EPF wage ceiling of Rs 25,000 per month under the Code on Social Security, replacing Rs 15,000 ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/09/19/labour-ministry-notifies-25000-wage-ceiling-under-social-security-code/)). It is not for us to say what caused the Government's decision, since several organisations had raised the ceiling, but the episode shows why a demand tied to a named number is easy to track and to compare with the outcome.

## Weak and strong demands

Weak: "Improve conditions of workers."

Strong: "Revise the monthly honorarium of mid-day meal cooks and helpers to not less than the State minimum wage for unskilled workers, with effect from 1 April."

The strong version has an identifiable group, a standard (the State minimum wage), and a date. It also fits the law. Under the Code on Wages, the minimum wages fixed by the Central or State Governments must be above the floor wage and must be reviewed at least every five years ([PRS summary of the Code on Wages](https://prsindia.org/billtrack/prs-products/prs-bill-summary-3305)). A memorandum that cites such a provision shows that the union has done its homework.

## Using the grievance portal alongside

For complaints about service delivery by central Government offices, the Government runs the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS), which is open 24 hours and gives each complaint a unique registration ID that can be used to track its status. If the outcome is closed with a rating of "Poor", the user can appeal. The portal does not take up matters that are in court, RTI matters, or most service matters of Government employees, and it states that grievances sent by email are not entertained ([CPGRAMS](https://pgportal.gov.in/)). A memorandum to a ministry and a CPGRAMS grievance are not rivals. The first sets out a policy demand, the second pursues a specific failure.

## When to escalate

If there is no reply, move up in stages. First, send a reminder to the same officer. Second, write to the next higher authority with a copy of the first memorandum. Third, involve your federation and the State or national leadership, and ask for the matter to be placed before the relevant tripartite committee or board. Fourth, publicise the demand through a press note and a meeting with legislators. Agitation is the last stage, not the first. BMS has said in its own statements that it favours constructive engagement with Government on pro-worker initiatives while objecting to policies that it considers harmful to workers ([BMS statement, 31 January 2026](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=9332)). A well-documented record of earlier steps strengthens the case if agitation does become necessary.

## A short checklist before you sign

- Is it addressed to the right authority, by designation?
- Does each demand name a specific action, a standard and a date?
- Are the facts accurate and the rules cited correctly?
- Are annexures attached and listed?
- Do you have a dated receipt copy, and a diary note to follow up?
